strengths: Compelling perceptual supervision strategy: Replacing standard low-level reconstruction objectives (L1, LPIPS) in the 3D lifting stage with feature-level supervision from foundational models (DINOv2 and SAM 2.1) is well-motivated and demonstrates clear improvements in semantic coherence and identity preservation under extreme viewpoints.

Strong extreme-view robustness: Both quantitative results (Table 1 & Table 2) and qualitative visualizations (Figure 3, Figure 8, Figure 9) convincingly show that PercHead handles steep side, overhead, and profile angles significantly better than recent baselines like GAGAvatar, LAM, and PanoHead, mitigating common artifacts such as facial collapsing or texture smearing.

Effective disentangled 3D editing framework: Adapting the architecture with FaRL semantic segmentation maps for geometry and CLIP embeddings for appearance enables intuitive, independent control over shape and style with zero-shot text conditioning and image-based transfer.

Comprehensive baseline comparison and informative ablations: The evaluation thoroughly benchmarks against pertinent 3D head reconstruction models (PanoHead, GAGAvatar, LAM, LGM) across Ava-256 and NeRSemble, accompanied by sensible ablations analyzing loss components and training data composition.
weaknesses: Reliance on a 2D CNN refiner: The final output relies on a post-rasterization 2D CNN refiner trained with LPIPS and L1. While it enhances sharpness, post-rendering 2D convolutions can undermine strict multi-view 3D consistency and function as a 2D neural upsampler rather than keeping the representation purely in 3D Gaussian space.

Relatively small quantitative evaluation set: The evaluation is conducted on only 11 identities from Ava-256 and 5 identities from NeRSemble. Evaluating across a larger collection of identities or conducting a user study on diverse in-the-wild portraits would provide more statistical weight to the perceptual superiority claims.

Metric trade-offs in loss ablations: In Table 3 without the CNN module ('LPIPS+L1 w.o. CNN' vs. 'Full w.o. CNN'), conventional supervision outperforms the proposed foundation model loss on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, winning primarily on DreamSim and ArcFace. A deeper technical analysis of these trade-offs and potential structural biases introduced by the foundation model encoders would strengthen the paper.

strengths: The paper introduces a coherent and well-motivated architecture combining a frozen DINOv2 backbone with a task-adaptive ViT encoder, followed by an iterative cross-attention decoder initialized from a canonical FLAME template to predict 3D Gaussians.

The exploration of supervising base 3D lifting using foundational model representations (intermediate DINOv2 features and SAM 2.1 embeddings) rather than pure pixel-wise or standard perceptual losses provides interesting empirical insights and yields robust reconstructions under large viewpoint deviations.

Comprehensive novel-view synthesis experiments against strong recent baselines (GAGAvatar, LAM, PanoHead, LGM) across Ava-256 and NeRSemble demonstrate competitive results, particularly regarding extreme view handling, perceptual metrics, and identity preservation (ArcFace).

The extension to semantic 3D editing via FaRL segmentation maps and CLIP style embeddings presents an intuitive way to disentangle structural geometry from style, supporting both image- and zero-shot text-driven manipulations.
weaknesses: Reliance on 2D CNN post-refinement: The pipeline relies on a shallow 2D CNN refiner applied after 3D Gaussian rasterization (supervised with standard L1/LPIPS). As shown in Table 3, the CNN significantly alters metrics. Applying 2D neural upsampling/refinement risks introducing multi-view inconsistencies and temporal flickering when camera trajectories are smoothly interpolated, yet multi-view consistency metrics across continuous camera orbits are not quantitatively benchmarked.

Absence of direct 3D geometric evaluation: While image-space novel-view synthesis and perceptual/identity metrics are reported, both Ava-256 and NeRSemble contain underlying 3D ground truth. The paper would be substantially stronger with direct 3D geometric error metrics (e.g., Chamfer distance, point-to-plane distance, or surface normal accuracy) to validate that the lifted 3D Gaussians yield accurate 3D geometry rather than relying heavily on the 2D post-processing network.

Small quantitative evaluation scale: The quantitative benchmarks are computed over a limited sample (11 identities from Ava-256 and 5 identities from NeRSemble), which leaves questions about statistical significance across wider demographic and appearance distributions.

Ablation analysis on loss formulation shows mixed outcomes: Without the 2D CNN, the standard LPIPS+L1 objective outperforms the proposed foundation loss on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS (Table 3), complicating the claim that foundation model supervision fundamentally supersedes conventional reconstruction objectives for 3D lifting.

strengths: The proposed supervision strategy using intermediate features from foundation models (DINOv2 and SAM 2.1) without relying on standard pixel-level reconstruction losses during the initial lifting stage is an insightful design choice that yields robust cross-view generalization.

Superior performance on extreme viewpoint novel-view synthesis: As demonstrated in both quantitative evaluations (Tables 1 and 2) and qualitative comparisons (Figures 3, 8, and 9), the model shows noticeable improvements in identity preservation (ArcFace) and perceptual metrics (LPIPS, DreamSim) when evaluated against strong baselines such as LAM, GAGAvatar, and PanoHead.

Effective disentanglement in 3D face editing: By utilizing FaRL segmentation maps for geometric layout and CLIP embeddings for appearance, the framework supports both zero-shot text-prompted and reference-image-driven 3D head editing with clean separation between shape and texture.

Efficient architecture choices, such as foreground patch masking (discarding background tokens to save up to 30% compute) and omitting expensive 3D-to-3D patch self-attention while achieving spatial coherence through iterative cross-attention to 2D features.
weaknesses: Reliance on 2D CNN post-processing: The Gaussian splatting output is refined by a shallow 2D CNN trained with standard L1 and LPIPS losses. Applying 2D image-space refinement is known to risk introducing multi-view inconsistencies or subtle flickering across views/frames. The paper lacks a quantitative analysis of cross-view consistency (e.g., cross-view flow error or warp consistency) to confirm whether the CNN degrades 3D consistency.

Nuance in the loss formulation claims: The paper argues that foundational model losses make conventional losses unnecessary; however, in Table 3 without the CNN ('w.o. CNN'), the baseline trained with LPIPS+L1 achieves superior PSNR (15.96 vs 15.94), SSIM (0.7228 vs 0.7089), and LPIPS (0.2897 vs 0.3010) compared to the proposed full loss without CNN. Moreover, the second-stage CNN refinement itself explicitly requires LPIPS and L1, which somewhat weakens the overarching claim.

Limited evaluation sample size: Quantitative evaluation is conducted on only 11 identities from Ava-256 and 5 identities from NeRSemble (16 test identities total). Evaluating on a broader identity set would provide stronger statistical confidence.

Computational overhead and interaction latency: As noted in the supplementary material, stylization takes 10 to 28 seconds and segmentation extraction requires 25 seconds. While acceptable for offline editing, it restricts the practical utility for interactive or real-time avatar applications.
